chunks: As for what al-Ḥusayn ibn Saʿīd narrated from Ibn Abī ʿUmayr, from Jamīl ibn Darrāj, from Abū Usāmah Zayd al-Shaḥḥām, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, concerning:

the mouse, the cat, the chicken, the dog, and the bird, he said: If it has not decomposed, or the taste of the water has not changed, then five buckets will suffice you. But if the water has changed, then draw from it until the odor goes away.

So this report also admits two possibilities: one of them is what we mentioned in the earlier reports, namely that he was answering about the ruling of the chicken and the bird. The second is that we understand it to mean that if the dog fell into it and came out alive, then this amount up to seven buckets is drawn from it; and there is nothing in the report indicating that it died in it. That which indicates this is what...

key_terms.الرِّيحُ: the odor whose disappearance marks the endpoint of drawing water
key_terms.الْفَأْرَةِ: the mouse mentioned among animals falling into the well
key_terms.الْكَلْبِ: the dog, whose case is specifically analyzed in the report
key_terms.حُكْمِ: the legal ruling being inferred from the narration
key_terms.خَمْسُ دِلَاءٍ: five buckets, the stated sufficient amount to draw in one case
key_terms.سَبْعِ دِلَاءٍ: seven buckets, the upper amount mentioned in the interpretive explanation
key_terms.طَعْمُ الْمَاءِ: the taste of the water as a sign of change affecting the ruling

ai.seo_question: How many buckets should be drawn from a well if a dog or other animal falls into it?
ai.summary: This passage discusses the legal ruling concerning a well into which certain animals have fallen. It indicates a measured amount of water to be drawn if the water's taste has not changed, and a greater removal if its smell changes, while the compiler notes possible interpretive readings of the report regarding the dog and other animals.
